parole.significato: Any of several species of Arctic sea birds of the family Alcidae.
parole.testo: From Icelandic álka, from Old Norse alka (“auk”), from Proto-Germanic *alkǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“a kind of bird”). Cognate with Swedish alka (“auk”), Norwegian and Danish alke (“auk”), Swedish dialectal alla (“long-tailed duck”) (Clangula hyemalis, syn. Fuligula glacialis), Latin olor

parole.significato: Chiefly in shipbuilding: to construct (a ship or part of it) using wooden boards or planks; to board, to plank.
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Icelandic byrði (“side of a ship, board”).

parole.significato: An Icelandic distilled beverage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic brennivín. Doublet of brandywine.

parole.significato: Any of the species of Somateria spp. and Polysticta stelleri or of the seaduck subfamily Merginae, which line their nes…
parole.testo: From Icelandic æðar, genitive of æðr, probably reaching English via Swedish eider (now ejder), from a North Germanic root.

parole.significato: A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of an Icelandic króna
parole.testo: From Icelandic eyrir. Doublet of aureus, öre, øre, and oyra.

parole.significato: A waterfall.
parole.testo: From Icelandic or Norwegian foss, both from Old Norse fors (“waterfall”). Doublet of force (“waterfall”).

parole.significato: A deity to whom one is wholeheartedly and/or exclusively devoted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic fulltrúi (“one who is fully trusted”).

parole.significato: Either of two species of pelagic seabird in the genus Fulmarus, Fulmarus glacialis and F. glacialoides, which breed on…
parole.testo: From Icelandic fúlmár, from Old Norse fúlmár, from Old Norse fúll (“foul”) + már (“gull, mew”) (see English mew), evidently in reference to the foul-smelling vomit it ejects to deter predators.

parole.significato: The great auk.
parole.testo: From Icelandic geirfugl, from Old Norse geirfugl (“great auk”), related to Swedish garfågel, Danish geirfugl, Faroese geirfuglur, gorfuglur, French gorfou.

parole.testo: From Icelandic Geysir (“Gusher”), the Icelandic name of a particular hot spring in Iceland (see Wikipedia), from the verb geysa (“to gush”), from Old Norse geysa (“to gush”), which is mentioned in English as early as the 1760s in The Annual Register, as “Geyser, a wonderful spring in the valley of H

parole.significato: A ball of moss, often surrounding a rock, that moves across a glacier.
parole.testo: Calque of Icelandic jökla-mýs. Coined by geologist Jón Eythórsson in 1950. The Icelandic term appears only in plural form.

parole.significato: A local chieftain in Norse societies, who held religious and administrative duties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic goði.

parole.significato: The state or authority of a godi
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic goðorð.

parole.significato: A priestess of the modern Norse religion.
parole.testo: From Icelandic gyðja.

parole.significato: A synonym used in Old Norse poetry in place of the normal word for something; a poetic epithet.
parole.testo: From Icelandic heiti, from Old Norse heiti, from Old Norse heita (“to be named”), from Proto-Germanic *haitaną (“to call, name, order”). Doublet of hight.

parole.significato: A sloping plain between mountain ridges.
parole.testo: From Icelandic hóp (“a small bay or inlet”). Cognate with English hoop.

parole.significato: An Icelandic food, cured fermented shark with a strong ammonia smell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic hákarl (“shark”).

parole.significato: A bird in genus Gavia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic himbrimi (“surf roarer”).

parole.significato: A mountain covered with ice and snow, a snow mountain.
parole.testo: From Icelandic jökull (“glacier”). Doublet of ickle.

parole.significato: A subglacial outburst flood; a sudden release of water from a subglacial lake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic jökulhlaup (“glacier burst”).

parole.significato: The currency of Iceland, divided into 100 aurar
parole.testo: From Icelandic and Faroese. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, krona, and krone.

parole.significato: Agonus cataphractus, a European fish having the body covered with bony plates, and with three spines projecting in fron…
parole.testo: From Icelandic hlýri.

parole.significato: A fabled marine male creature usually represented as having the head, trunk, and arms of a man and a lower part like th…
parole.testo: From Icelandic and Old Norse.

parole.significato: A pair of pants made from the skin of the lower half (below the waist) of a dead man, used by medieval Icelandic sorcer…
parole.testo: From necro- + pants, a calque of Icelandic nábrók.

parole.significato: Among the early and medieval Teutonic peoples, especially Scandinavians, the heritable land held by the various odalmen…
parole.testo: From Icelandic óðal (“estate”). Cognate with Norwegian odel, odal (“allodium, patrimony”), Old English ēþel (“homeland”). Compare athel, Odelsthing.

parole.significato: A plain created by the outwash of glacial meltwater.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic sandur (“sand”). Doublet of sand.

parole.significato: To skimp; to do something in a skimpy or slipshod fashion.
parole.testo: Perhaps related to sense 1, but influenced by the later attested skimp; however, compare Icelandic skamta (“to dole out, to stint”), which is related to skammur (“short”).

parole.significato: A boat; a small vessel.
parole.testo: From Icelandic skúta; akin to Swedish skuta, Danish skude, Dutch schuit.

parole.significato: A yogurt-like product made of curdled milk, curds stored up for food; a thick dairy product unique to Icelandic cuisine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic skyr.

parole.significato: A fibrous brown coal or bituminous wood.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic surtarbrandr (“black firebrand”).

parole.significato: An elongate ridge of pyroclastic palagonitic tuff, lava delta hyaloclastites, and pillow lavas common in Iceland, erupt…
parole.testo: Coined by American volcanologist John Gilbert Jones in 1968, after the Icelandic word Icelandic tindur (“pinnacle, peak”), although its plural form, tindar has, since Jones' coinage, been used incorrectly as the singular.

parole.significato: The hedge sparrow, dunnock, titlene, Prunella modularis.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Superficially tit (“a small bird”) + -ling (“small”). Attested from the 16th century. Probably from Icelandic titlingr (“tit sparrow”), Old Norse titlingr (“sparrow”). Compare Old Norse tittr (“titmouse”). Also see Middle English titmose (“titmouse”).

parole.significato: A four-beat lateral ambling gait mainly found in Icelandic horses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Icelandic tölt.

parole.significato: Allodial, inalienable.
parole.testo: From Icelandic óðal. More at odal.

parole.significato: The pectoral fin of a fish.
parole.testo: From Icelandic uggi (“fin”).

parole.significato: The dealfish, Trachipterus arcticus
parole.testo: From Icelandic vagmeri (“flounder”, literally “wave mare”).

parole.significato: A dessert of cake with layers of prune filling.
parole.testo: From Icelandic vínarterta.

parole.significato: An ice-covered volcano in Iceland.
parole.testo: Icelandic jökull (“glacier”). Doublet of ickle.

parole.significato: One of several trolls, children of the ogress Grýla, who, according to Icelandic folktales, arrive one each day from De…
parole.testo: Calque of Icelandic jólasveinn. Compare also Yule swain.
